task_brief: Day 6 of "Debugging, Testing, and Version Control" (unit 3, grade 9) is a correction and reflection on debugging, testing, and version control. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Repair a supplied defective program and deliver a commit history, a defect log, a failing test that reproduces the bug, and a verified fix. Today's work contributes to that by handling debugging, testing, and version control at the correction and reflection stage, against the unit's wider topics of defect classes and error messages, reading traces and diagnostic output, systematic debugging strategy, and version control commits and history. This session produces reviewable evidence toward the unit performance task.
primary_task: Correct and reflect on your own earlier work involving debugging, testing, and version control. Build a defect log: one row per error, giving the symptom you or the check observed, the root cause you diagnosed, the specific change that fixed it, and the check that now passes. Include at least one case that failed before the fix and passes after it. Then write what pattern connects your errors — a misread condition, a skipped verification, an assumption about debugging, testing, and version control — and name one habit that would catch that pattern earlier next time. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about debugging, testing, and version control, and it belongs to "Debugging, Testing, and Version Control", which also covers separate topics such as defect classes and error messages. Close out with this check before you stop: For one corrected item, state the original error, its cause, and the check that would catch it next time. At grade 9 the bar is independent work with explicit criteria set before you start, and evidence that you evaluated the finished result against those criteria rather than against how it felt.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, score excerpt, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting debugging, testing, and version control.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile or concrete model, or adult demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for debugging, testing, and version control follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for debugging, testing, and version control, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to debugging, testing, and version control works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of debugging, testing, and version control, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking debugging, testing, and version control mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply debugging, testing, and version control under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on debugging, testing, and version control rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
